segments.text: We know that AI converts text into tokens, and each token is assigned a unique token ID.
But a token ID is simply a number.
On its own, that number does not contain or explain any information about what the token actually means.
An ID identifies you. It doesn't describe you.
Think of a cafeteria.
The numbers on these student badges tell you which student is which.
They tell you nothing about who each student is, like whether they are funny, play hockey,
or the person who steals french fries at lunch.
To see how numbers can represent meaning, let's look at this table for a beverage taste test.
We will rate drinks across six specific characteristics.
Sweet, bitter, fizz, heat, caffeine, and dark.
Each receives a score from zero to ten.
A higher number means more of that trait.
A single ID number cannot describe a complex student, and a single number is not enough for an AI to understand a word.
But by using a structured array of numbers across multiple distinct traits, we can create a measurable profile.
You and your friends tasted coffee and rated it on six characteristics.
Let's put those ratings in the table.
Coffee scores one for sweet, nine for bitter, zero for fizz, nine for heat, eight for caffeine, and ten for dark.
Next, you rate Coke on the same six characteristics.
Nine, one, ten, two, three, and eight.
Which drink scores nine sweet, one bitter, and ten fizz?
That's Coke.
A row of numbers like this is a vector.
Each position is a dimension, and its number is the value.
This vector functions as a mathematical fingerprint.
It gives us a shared standardized language of data,
allowing us to accurately compare completely different items.
Now let's add Pepsi to our taste test.
Look closely at its ratings.
All six of its values match Coke exactly.
If you hid the names of the drinks and only looked at these numbers, you physically could not tell Coke and Pepsi apart.
Citrus gives us a seventh dimension.
We will now rate each drink for citrus flavor on the exact same zero to ten scale.
Coffee scores a zero for citrus, Coke scores one, and Pepsi scores ten.
The first six values for the two sodas still match, but their seven number profiles now differ.
Another dimension can capture a difference the earlier numbers missed.
As the items we are comparing increase in complexity and nuance, we must continually add dimensions.
This is the only way to ensure every unique item has a truly distinct factor.
This table compares our taste test with how an AI operates.
Just as each drink has a numeric profile, every token in the AI's vocabulary has its own row of numbers.
That row is called an embedding.
The scale, however, is much larger.
Instead of tracking three drinks across seven dimensions,
AI models map every single token across typically thousands of dimensions.
And instead of human-named traits rated from zero to ten,
the AI uses unlabeled positive and negative decimals.
It learns these values during training to map patterns and how each token is used.
In both systems, complex characteristics are distilled into a mathematical sequence.
This diagram shows the inside of a real model.
When you type the word cat, the AI finds its token ID, which is 4719.
That ID leads directly to the token's row in the embedding table,
sitting alongside other tokens like dog, latte, and bicycle.
Look at the columns labeled D1 through DN.
Cats row begins with 0.45, then negative 0.23, 0.80, and continues across thousands of positions.
A single learned number in this sequence is a parameter,
and the complete row is the embedding.
This applies to everything the AI processes.
Even fragments of words, like the un, believe, and wobble in unbelievable,
receive their own unique embeddings of learned numbers.
By translating abstract concepts into a mathematical format,
these models can effectively evaluate complex relationships.
